normalization: Project Gutenberg texts stripped at the START/END markers, CRLF to LF, otherwise unaltered; Internet Archive OCR text layers as fetched, uncorrected (text/<slug>.ocr.txt) — the scan under original/<identifier>/ is the witness; Ganjoor JSON as fetched, rendered one couplet per line, hemistichs joined by ' / ', section titles marked '=== title ==='.
scope: Pearl, Cleanness and Patience in their first edition, with the manuscript itself in the 1923 facsimile, and Gollancz's Pearl of 1891 with its modern rendering on the facing page. Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, the fourth poem of Cotton Nero A.x, is in the facsimile and not otherwise seated in this pass: QUEUED (Morris, EETS o.s. 4, 1864, is public domain). Modern editions (Gordon 1953; Andrew and Waldron) are in copyright and are not seated. St. Erkenwald, sometimes given to the same poet, is in another manuscript and is not seated.
verified_loci: Pearl, line 1 — 'Perle plesau{n}te to prynces paye' (the expansions of the manuscript's abbreviations, italic in Morris, are marked with braces in the Gutenberg text)
Pearl, line 1212, the last — 'Ande precio{us} perleȝ vnto his pay. Amen. Amen.'
Gollancz 1891, line 1 — the text layer reads 'ERLE plesaunte to prynces paye' (the drop capital is lost; the scan is the witness)
why_seated: The poem whose name the archive's own Pearl and Other Poems (2014) carries, seated so the name has its source on the shelf. A father who has lost a pearl in the grass, his daughter, dead before she was two, falls asleep where it fell and sees her across a river in the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21: the archive's Revelation line meets it there.
